description_full: Diana Shipping Inc. provides shipping transportation services worldwide. It also engages in the ownership and bareboat charter-in of dry bulk carriers. The company transports a range of dry bulk cargoes, including commodities, such as iron ore, coal, grain, and other materials in shipping routes. December 31, 2025, the company had a fleet of 36 dry bulk carriers, owned and chartered-in, consisting of nineUltramax, five Panamax, six Kamsarmax, four Post-Panamax, eight Capesize and four Newcastlemaxvessels, having a combined carrying capacity of approximately 4.1 million dwt. The company was formerly known as Diana Shipping Investments Corp. and changed its name to Diana Shipping Inc. in February 2005. Diana Shipping Inc. was incorporated in 1999 and is based in Athens, Greece.
ceo_bio: Ms. Semiramis  Paliou | CEO & Director | Age 50
financial_summary: Diana Shipping inc. is a micro-cap industrials business with a $296M market cap on $214M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -10% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are expanding by +2.1pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $46M in free cash flow — roughly 21 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.66× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.3× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 1.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 9.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 43% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 11pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.77x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 63% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 26% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 46% and a beta of 0.89, it moves roughly with the market.
About $2.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 59% in the 2020 crash, 42% in the 2022 bear market and 78% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 74% below its DCF fair value of $9.29, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 73%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $6.53 to $13.19 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 4.9 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 9.0 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 6.5 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 48% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 15.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $3.80 on average, 60% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.6%, so growth at these returns destroys value.
It converts 21% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.66x.
ROE of 4% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 46pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.3x net debt to EBITDA ($50.5M of cash against $522.8M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.0x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of -0.03 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -9.7% over 3 years, 4.7% over 5 years and 3.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 24%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 21.8% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.0x depreciation (0.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 42.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 15%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (18 sales, net $56.8M sold).
It returns 9.3% a year to shareholders (7.8% in buybacks and 1.7% in dividends).
The share count has grown 5.3% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
